page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.g9a.large is a general-purpose virtual machine instance hosted on the KVM hypervisor. It is powered by an AMD EPYC 9T25 processor based on the x86_64 architecture, clocked at a frequency of 2.7 GHz. The hardware configuration provisions 2 dedicated vCPUs paired with 8.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a 1:4 processor-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU.

The instance provides a baseline network throughput of 2 Gbps and includes zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. Local storage is not bundled with the instance, requiring storage capacity to be provisioned via external attached block volumes. Furthermore, the configuration excludes GPU hardware accelerators. Compute performance remains predictable due to the dedicated vCPU allocation rather than a burstable or shared-core model.

In terms of qualitative cost efficiency, the absence of onboard NVMe drives and accelerator modules minimizes unnecessary hardware overhead for baseline compute tasks. The balanced resource configuration makes Alibaba Cloud ecs.g9a.large suitable for standard operational workloads, including small-scale web serving, microservices, low-traffic application backends, and continuous integration environments.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.g9a.large is a general-purpose instance powered by an AMD EPYC 9T25 processor running on the KVM hypervisor with x86_64 architecture. Operating at 2.7 GHz, it provides 2 dedicated vCPUs and 8.0 GB of memory, yielding a 1:4 compute-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local storage, requiring network-attached storage for persistent disks, and operates without GPU acceleration. Network performance is provisioned at a 2 Gbps baseline bandwidth, with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses included. The dedicated compute allocation avoids noisy-neighbor throttling common in shared-core instances while maintaining low infrastructure overhead. This instance is best suited for entry-level general-purpose deployments, such as lightweight web servers, background task workers, microservices, and development environments.
